title: The Chariot Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Chariot upright: determination, direction, momentum; reversed: stalling or forcing it. Love, work, advice and Waite's 1911 text. Ask your question.
image_alt: The Chariot, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a crowned young man in armor stands in a stone chariot under a starry canopy, a black and a white sphinx lying in front of it.
capsule: The Chariot is card VII of the Major Arcana: victory through determination, direction and momentum held together by will. Reversed, it means lost control, stalling or aggression. It is a strong, encouraging card if you know your direction. The driver moves forward on focus alone, without reins, and the upright answer to yes or no is yes.

blocks.heading: What is on The Chariot card?
paragraphs: A young man in armor stands in a square stone chariot under a canopy covered with stars, a long staff in his right hand. Waite explains that "two sphinxes thus draw his chariot" (p. 96). On the 1909 card they lie in front of it, the one on the left black, the one on the right white, and no reins run from them to his hands.

Waite's text (p. 96) gives him "a drawn sword", but on the 1909 card what he holds looks more like a long staff or sceptre than a sword. Two yellow crescents sit on his shoulders and a bright square on his breastplate. About the shoulders Waite says only that "on the shoulders of the victorious hero are supposed to be the Urim and Thummim" (p. 96).

The front of the chariot carries a red emblem on a white shield, with blue wings spread above it. Behind him lies a walled town with red roofs under a yellow sky, and the numeral VII stands above the canopy.

Older decks drew the team differently. Waite notes that in the eighteenth century "white horses were yoked to the car", and that other animals, "a lion and a leopard" among them, were also used (pp. 15, 16).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Chariot?
paragraphs: Waite's upright list starts with help ("succour" means aid) and providence, then turns to conflict and to pride: "presumption" is taking more for granted than you should. The reversed list stays with friction: quarrels, disputes, losing ground.

He saw more in the card than that list. For him the charioteer is "above all things triumph in the mind", yet with a limit: the planes of his conquest are "manifest or external and not within himself" (p. 96). In Part I he says the card is "really the King in his triumph" (p. 15).

blocks.heading: What does The Chariot mean upright?
paragraphs: Determination drives The Chariot upright: a goal you have chosen and the will to keep moving toward it. Its usual modern meaning is victory won through effort: ambition, control over a situation, obstacles overcome because you kept going. It tends to appear when you have plenty of energy but need direction, or when two parts of you want different things and the road ahead needs both of them pulling together.

The picture shows how. No reins run from the driver's hands, so the sphinxes are steered by focus and self-control rather than by force. One is black and one is white; you are not asked to pick one of them, only to point both the same way.

That is where the momentum comes from. Waite's list has both triumph and presumption in it, and the modern reading keeps both: a strong run can tip into pushing too hard. When that feels familiar, the question to sit with is: where am I heading, and what in me is pulling the other way?

blocks.heading: What does The Chariot mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Chariot means a loss of control or direction. Often it shows momentum stalling because your energy is pulled two ways at once: scattered energy, too many goals, no single road, or obstacles that halt the advance. The other version is the opposite: forcing your way on, even with aggression, pushing so hard that you lose sight of where you meant to go.
Waite's reversed list of quarrels, disputes and defeat describes the outer side of this, a struggle with other people. Losing direction inside yourself is a modern reading, not Waite's.
Either way, what helps is steering, not speed. Stop for a moment, check the direction, and drop one thing that pulls against it before you add more force.

blocks.heading: What does The Chariot mean in love?
paragraphs: Knowing what you want and moving toward it with intention is what The Chariot asks of you in love, instead of waiting for your doubts to settle on their own. With no partner yet, the card may point to a clearer picture of what you want in someone and the nerve to act on it.

For a couple, the card means determination to make it work: getting through obstacles together and moving the relationship forward on purpose. The question is direction: where the relationship is heading and whether your own wishes have a place on that road.

When it comes up reversed, it can mean a relationship pulling in two directions, a power struggle, or one person trying to steer everything. On your side, notice whether you want closeness and freedom at once, or push a connection faster than feels right to you. What would it look like to slow down and steer?

blocks.heading: What does The Chariot mean for work and money?
paragraphs: A clear goal and steady effort are what The Chariot backs in your work: a project you drive to the finish, a push to get something moving, a decision about which way your work should go. It asks you to say no to tasks that pull against that goal.
Financially, The Chariot means discipline in the service of a goal: money brought under control, a clear target, progress earned by steady effort rather than luck.
Reversed, notice a plan that has stalled because it tries to go everywhere at the same time, or spending that runs without a direction.

blocks.heading: What is The Chariot's advice?
paragraphs: Pick the one direction that matters most right now and turn down one thing that pulls against it. Steer before you speed up: write the goal in a single line, then let that line decide what gets your time today.

blocks.heading: Is The Chariot a yes or no card?
The Chariot as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Someone driven and focused, who sets a course and keeps to it, fits The Chariot as a figure; drawn for yourself, it marks your readiness to take charge of where things go. As an answer about feelings, the card traditionally means determination and clear intent: interest that turns into action, a wish to move the connection forward and work through whatever stands in the way, sometimes with emotions kept under tight control. Reversed, it describes feelings in conflict: wanting closeness and freedom at once, frustration that the bond is not moving, like revving an engine that will not go, or an urge to control the pace.

pairs.text: Will meets patience. Keep moving forward, but steer with a gentle hand instead of a tight grip.
Momentum doubled: things are moving fast. Keep your eyes on the destination so that speed does not choose it for you.
Drive held up by an unmade choice. Decide first, and the motion will follow.
Motion beside stillness. A short stop to check your inner compass makes the next push count.

blocks.heading: The Chariot or the Six of Wands?
paragraphs: Both cards show a figure moving in triumph. The Six of Wands shows "a laurelled horseman" with footmen at his side, and Waite reads it on the surface as "a victor triumphing" (p. 186); the modern meaning is recognition, success that others can see. The Chariot is the drive that comes before: the will and the steering that get you there. If your question is whether your effort is noticed, look to the Six; if it is whether you can hold your course, it belongs to The Chariot.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Chariot
paragraphs: Where do I actually want to go, in one sentence?
Which two parts of me are pulling in different directions?
What could I drop so that my energy moves one way?

faq.q: Is The Chariot a good or bad card?
faq.a: More good than bad: it backs effort, focus and the decision to get moving, and often marks steady progress. The risk sits in the same engine: drive that forgets its destination turns into stubbornness, and Waite's own list mixes triumph with pride and conflict.

faq.q: Why does The Chariot have sphinxes instead of horses?
faq.a: Because Waite chose them. He writes that the hero "has thus replied to the sphinx" and that for this reason he "accepted the variation of Éliphas Lévi" (p. 96). In Part I he also warns that the sphinxes should not be taken for the card's original form (p. 15).

Not on its own. None of Waite's divinatory words for the Chariot is about a journey, and Arcana Diary reads the chariot as inner movement: a course you choose and hold. If you ask about a trip, the card speaks to how settled your decision feels, not to the trip itself.

faq.q: Is The Chariot a card of victory?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the classic victory cards: success won by focus and will rather than luck. Waite called the charioteer "conquest on all planes" but saw a limit too: the freedom he wins "may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding" (pp. 96–99). As a meaning, it describes the drive behind a win, not a promise about how any contest ends.

waite.quote: Succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble. Reversed: Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat.
